Located just off the side street from Yulgok, Onion is a bakery cafe that is located in what looks like was a former temple, and it has kept the design and fee of the area.

They are typically very busy, particularly as it gets after 10am and onwards, people will start lining up for the bread, drinks, and also the feel of the place.

First, due to the area seeming like a former temple, there’s a nice middle area that is just kept very simple, almost like a Zen garden feel.

The entry way and a he bakery are of course operationalized and not of the old temple like feel to it. The front door is where the counter is to pay and such, but to the side of the front door you will need to walk left to get to the bread and baked goods. While they don’t have a huge selection, they have a plentiful variety of different breads. Again, won’t be as much as you may have hoped for, but on par with most smaller bakeries.

Price wise, probably a bit more expensive than other spots, even more so than the more mainstream Paris Bageutte and Tous Les Jour, but not by too much all things considered.

The sitting areas here are all interesting, as there are areas that have that old school bamboo mat fee to them, they have seating that’s in a hallway wooden floor setting like the ones you see in movies where someone will clean it with a rag hunched over moving back and forth. And of course for those not as adventurous they have just standard seating and tables. A seat and area to appeal to all.

The breads I got today were both quite tasty. I think the one I liked better was the dark chocolate croissant, which was flaky, perfectly sweet, and just had that nice doughy texture on the inside. Will definitely get this again if I’m back.

I would recommend visiting Onion, if not for the experience alone of this kind of seating setting, but they also offer delicious baked goods on top of that. I’ll maybe try a drink there next time too.

A friend and I stopped here for lunch during our exploration of Bukchon. We were in the mood for Western food and this charming two-story restaurant proved to be an excellent choice. The first floor features a coffee shop and bakery with myriad tempting pastries. Stairs lead to the casual second-floor dining room and outside terrace. At 2 p.m., customers sat at only two tables in the dining room so the space offered a quiet, relaxing atmosphere, away from the hordes of tourists outside.

A greeter showed us to a table by the windows, which face the street, and gave us English menus. Offerings included a 3-course daily special, pasta, pizza, fish, meat, soup and small plates. We opted to share one of the salads and ordered two bruschettas topped with salmon and avocado. The tasty salad came loaded with fresh ingedients and nicely dressed. I considered the  bruschetta to be heavenly and especially enjoyed the black bread with purple crust. Squid ink contributed to its list of ingredients.

Service was European style — professional and impeccable. We needed to signal when ready for the bill. Otherwise, we could have lingered as long as we wanted to do so. 

When we left around 3 p.m., customers almost filled the first floor. It looked like a wonderful place to take a break from visiting nearby palaces and gawking at traditional architecture.

The full name of this place is 1 in 1 jan ( il-in il-jan / 1인1잔 ) at the Eunpyeong Hanok Village. 

The staff was kind and hard working. The place also has a good view. Other than that, I'd like to give my personal opinion about this place for anyone looking to come here, since I didn't read much into it before coming.

In fact, I had no idea this place is talked about on IG, TT and blogs. Had I known that beforehand, I probably would have avoided it because I usually don't trust social media cafes. It did explain the huge influx of visitors, though.

I've been to a lot of large cafes like this in Korea and this experience was a bit unfortunate due to the design, price and quality.

For starters, I've never been to a 5 story cafe that doesn't have an elevator. You gotta walk up the very, very narrow stairs. This combined with, as I mentioned, due to word online this is apparently a very popular place for tourists visiting the hanok mile. So there were actually times where I had to stand at the stairs and wait for a group of like 6+ people to all walk up the stairs, and then people at the bottom had to wait for me to walk down. The line area for the bathroom is also very narrow, so while I was waiting for someone who had clogged the toilet with toilet paper on accident, I had to allow people walking by to squeeze by and maneuver through. It was really weird and uncomfortable, and pretty poor design planning.

Also, this is important, though it is 5 stories, you're only allowed on the 3rd, 4th and 5th stories if you purchase a certain menu. If you're just there for coffee, you're limited to the first and second stories. The second story has a good view, but I guess people wanna come for a better one up top. Had I known that before coming, I probably would have gone elsewhere. Again, I didn't do much planning.

Third, the ice americano was 6,000 won (around $6) and rather than call it coffee, I'd rather refer to it as "coffee flavored water." If I pay that much for coffee I expect it to blow me away but I actually was so disappointed that when I got home I made myself a cup of McDonalds decaf just so I could taste coffee again. I'm not saying that McDonalds decaf is the epitome of coffee, I'm making the point that it is what I had to do to enjoy the flavor of coffee for the day. In addition from what I saw, non-coffee drinks like ades and such were at least 7,5000 won (around $7.50) but luckily we didn't buy that.

Finally, the space is cramped. Remember I mentioned the huge groups of tourists? There's not enough space for everyone to walk around the seats so people are regularly maneuvering to let others through. Not sure what the 3rd-5th stories look like, but when we walked into the place after seeing pics we were like, "This is it?"

Lastly, parking is essentially non existent for customers. I did already have a concern about this so it is what it is, but I parked for a fee at the museum and I'm pretty sure they ripped us off as we were leaving. 

Anyway, if you like social media cafes and want some decent pics and don't care about flavor, this place might be fine for you. I just wanted some coffee and a chill atmosphere. Though again, the staff was cool. No disrespect.

You go in and realise quite quickly that most of the people at the tables and lining up at the counter are… mannequins. They are eating plastic fries. Everywhere you look, something odd is going on. 

Downstairs, Nudake has strange cakes. They are expensive and weird, but everyone buys them and they taste pretty good, if you love cream. There’s A LOT of cream. If you are lactose intolerant, maybe this isn’t the best place for you. 

You line up for a table, and somewhere along the line, you get to key in your orders on an iPad. Don’t expect much service. You are left to figure out the system and if you ask a staff they will probably tell you the wrong thing. We asked and were told there’s no queue; just find a table and sit, the guy said. BUT, there clearly was a queue, a long one, and it’s a good thing we decided to join it because we don’t like angry people yelling at us. 

There are plastic versions of the cakes on display, like in an art gallery. There’s several large screens scattered about showing people in repetitive motions. There’s one with a guy waving a plastic arm. There’s another with a creepy old guy eating cream. Maybe it’s installation art. It’s a little unnerving but nevermind… just focus on the cakes. 

The drinks are also good. My coffee had ice that looks like a part of a face. You pour milk over the face and watch it melt. It tasted fine. The matcha latte was pretty and tasty. 

They change their cakes so there’s no point telling you about them; you will probably get something else that’s weird.

It may looks a bit messy however at the same time artistic in some way haha. This cold coffee has infused with butterscotch candies, thus it carries a hint of buttery and caramel flavours. Since there are tons of cream as well, I think the coffee taste has slightly overshadowed by other flavours.

I have convinced my friend to get a Cremart, basically it is a coffee topped with cream. Yet the barista has brought some uniquenesses to it, which he draws a lovely baby face on the cream. After taking dozens of photos, I finally have a sip of the drink, the cream is quite thick on the surface, guess that’s how they can stabilize the cremart? You can taste a stronger coffee flavour in this one and the cream has added a sweetness to the coffee.

Besides than drinks, the only food that they serve here is tiramisu and because we are both matcha lovers, we have chosen Matcha Tiramisu. It doesn’t look like a regular tiramisu, by that I mean it doesn’t look like a cake. The lady finger biscuits have soaked up with coffee, next topped with matcha flavoured mascarpone cheese. Seoul is overflowing with coffeeshop chains that will serve up the usual fare. They were uniformly acceptable and predictable in what they offered, but it’s nice to indulge a coffee snob’s palate if that’s one of your vices. I had got a list together of ‘third wave’ establishments in Seoul prior to my trip, but they are a little more spread out than I had anticipated. I eventually made it to this place on my last day in the city and I’m thankful I did. There’s not a lot to say, other than the pour-over black filter was fantastic – a sure sign that they know what they are doing. On my way out I eyed the beans they had for sale, and seeing that a 300g bag was less than £10 (with Won purchased pre-Brexit) I picked up a bag. They even threw in a small sample of some award winning beans they’d roasted that was good for two cups. It was the best coffee I’ve made at home in a long time, far better than most beans I’ve picked up in London over the past few years.

It was a midweek afternoon and there was plenty of seating available in the upstairs area, but I’m not sure what it would be like during a busier period. Decor is modern and inoffensive. They have plenty of awards on display downstairs – no doubt justified. It would make for a perfect ending to a few hours walking from Bukchon Hanok Village through Insadong.

For our 'main course' we were allowed to pick any specialty drink on their menu.  I was tired and wanted something comforting so I ordered the Soul Chai.  The tea was the warm hug I imagined.  Others were a little more adventurous and ended up with some really incredible creations.
